root.title: Nonsmooth Equation Local-Model Calculus
root.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth equation representations, map structures, generalized linearizations, local regularity, Newton approximation families, local convergence mechanisms, equation merits, and root certificates. General variational-analysis foundations, full globalization algorithms, smoothing and interior methods, function-space theory, and general numerical linear algebra remain outside this chapter.

children.title: Equation Reformulation Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Canonical systems represented as nonsmooth equations and the relationships among competing residual formulations.

children.title: Direct Residual Equations
children.top_down_role: Single-valued residual systems classified by dimension and parameter dependence.

children.title: Square Nonsmooth Equations
children.top_down_role: Residual systems with equally dimensioned variables and equations.

knowledge_statements.title: Square Nonsmooth Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional square residual systems, the setting for generalized-Jacobian Newton models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A square nonsmooth equation is a system \[F(x)=0,\] where \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of a point of interest. A solution is any \(x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(F(x^*)=0\). For a local Newton model at \(x\), one selects a generalized derivative matrix \(V\in\partial F(x)\) and seeks a step \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \[Vd=-F(x).\] The equal domain and codomain dimensions make nonsingularity of \(V\) a meaningful local solvability condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square nonsmooth equation has equally many variables and residual components; generalized derivative matrices are square and can define Newton steps when nonsingular.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz near the point considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x^*)=0\), with local model \(Vd=-F(x)\) for \(V\in\partial F(x)\).

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of the locally Lipschitz residual

children.title: Rectangular Nonsmooth Equations
children.top_down_role: Overdetermined and underdetermined residual systems requiring compatibility, least-squares, or minimum-norm interpretations.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Nonsmooth Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional overdetermined and underdetermined locally Lipschitz residual systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rectangular nonsmooth equation is \[F(x)=0,\] with locally Lipschitz \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(m\ne n\). If \(m>n\), exact solvability requires compatibility of the residual components; absent an exact zero, a standard interpretation minimizes \(\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert^2\). If \(m<n\), exact solutions may be nonunique; a selected solution may minimize a prescribed norm or regularizer over \(F^{-1}(0)\). A generalized linear model uses \(Vd=-F(x)\) with \(V\in\partial F(x)\), interpreted as a least-squares or minimum-norm system when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rectangular residual systems have unequal numbers of equations and variables, requiring compatibility, least-squares, or minimum-norm interpretations according to their dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=0\) is interpreted exactly when compatible, otherwise through an explicitly chosen least-squares or minimum-norm criterion.

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian, consisting of rectangular matrices

children.title: Parameterized Residual Equations
children.top_down_role: Perturbed equation families used in local stability and sensitivity analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Residual Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed finite-dimensional residual families and their local solution mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be a parameter set. A parameterized residual equation is \[F(x,p)=0,\qquad (x,p)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times P,\] where \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times P\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuous and locally Lipschitz in \(x\) near a reference pair \((\bar x,\bar p)\) satisfying \(F(\bar x,\bar p)=0\). Its solution mapping is \[S(p):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:F(x,p)=0\}.\] Local stability and sensitivity concern the behavior of \(S(p)\) near \((\bar p,\bar x)\) under perturbations of \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized residual equation defines a family of zero sets and a solution mapping whose local response to parameter perturbations is studied.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its decision variable near \((\bar x,\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(p)=\{x:F(x,p)=0\}\) is the associated parameter-dependent solution mapping.

children.title: Variational-Inequality Residuals
children.top_down_role: Equation reformulations generated from projection and normal-map representations of variational inequalities.

children.title: Natural Residual Equations
children.top_down_role: Projection-based residual formulations for constrained variational systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural Residual Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection residual representation of a variational inequality over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\gamma>0\). Define the natural residual by \[R_\gamma(x):=x-P_C\bigl(x-\gamma F(x)\bigr),\qquad x\in C.\] Then \[R_\gamma(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle F(x),y-x\rangle\ge 0\ \text{for every }y\in C.\] Thus zeros of the projection-based residual are exactly solutions of the variational inequality \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point solves the variational inequality exactly when it is fixed by the projected forward step, equivalently when its natural residual vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\gamma(x)=0\iff x\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\).

notation.meaning: variational inequality defined by C and F

children.title: Normal-Map Equations
children.top_down_role: Normal-map reformulations and their local piecewise-smooth structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Map Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-map reformulation of a variational inequality, including its polyhedral piecewise-smooth structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and let \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n\). Define \[F_C^{\mathrm{nor}}(z):=F(P_Cz)+z-P_Cz.\] Then \[F_C^{\mathrm{nor}}(z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x:=P_Cz\ \text{solves }\operatorname{VI}(C,F),\] with the inverse correspondence \(z=x-F(x)\). If \(C\) is polyhedral and \(F\) is continuously differentiable, then \(P_C\) is piecewise affine and \(F_C^{\mathrm{nor}}\) is locally piecewise continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal-map zero in the unconstrained variable corresponds exactly to a variational-inequality solution; polyhedral projection gives a piecewise-smooth local equation.
assumptions_latex: For the structural claim, \(C\) is polyhedral and \(F\) is continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C^{\mathrm{nor}}(z)=0\iff P_Cz\in\operatorname{SOL}(C,F)\), and the normal map is piecewise continuously differentiable under the stated structural assumptions.

notation.meaning: normal map associated with C and F

children.title: Proximal Residuals
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point residual representations induced by proximal mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-proximal residual for a smooth-plus-convex generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and choose \(\lambda>0\). Define \[R_\lambda^{\mathrm{prox}}(x):=x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr).\] Then \[R_\lambda^{\mathrm{prox}}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in F(x)+\partial g(x).\] Hence the generalized equation is represented exactly by the zero set of a single-valued proximal residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward-proximal fixed-point residual vanishes exactly at solutions of the inclusion involving the field and the convex subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\lambda^{\mathrm{prox}}(x)=0\iff 0\in F(x)+\partial g(x)\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of lambda times g

children.title: Resolvent Residuals
children.top_down_role: Fixed-point residual representations induced by resolvent mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-resolvent residual for generalized equations governed by a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be maximal monotone, let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and choose \(\lambda>0\). With \(J_{\lambda A}:=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\), define \[R_\lambda^{A}(x):=x-J_{\lambda A}\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr).\] The resolvent is single-valued on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and \[R_\lambda^{A}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in F(x)+A(x).\] Thus the generalized equation is equivalent to a nonsmooth residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized equation with a maximal monotone operator is equivalent to the vanishing of its forward-resolvent fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\lambda^{A}(x)=0\iff 0\in F(x)+A(x)\).

children.title: Proximal–Resolvent Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Representation links between proximal residuals and resolvent residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal–Resolvent Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of convex proximal mappings with subdifferential resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). Then \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}=(I+\lambda\partial g)^{-1}=J_{\lambda\partial g}.\] Consequently, for every mapping \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), the proximal and resolvent residuals coincide pointwise: \[x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr)=x-J_{\lambda\partial g}\bigl(x-\lambda F(x)\bigr).\] Their common zero set is exactly \(\{x:0\in F(x)+\partial g(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, its proximal mapping is the resolvent of its subdifferential, so the corresponding residual equations are identical.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}=J_{\lambda\partial g}\), and the induced proximal and resolvent residuals coincide.

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of lambda times g

children.title: Parameterization Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Effects of primitive parameters on residual geometry and local scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterization Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz sensitivity of a fixed-operator resolvent residual to perturbations of its forward field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\), let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be maximal monotone, let \(\lambda>0\), and let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times P\to\mathbb{R}^n\). Define \[R_\lambda(x,p):=x-J_{\lambda A}\bigl(x-\lambda F(x,p)\bigr).\] Because \(J_{\lambda A}\) is nonexpansive, for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(p,q\in P\), \[\lVert R_\lambda(x,p)-R_\lambda(x,q)\rVert\le\lambda\lVert F(x,p)-F(x,q)\rVert.\] Hence, if \(F(x,\cdot)\) is locally \(L_p\)-Lipschitz uniformly for nearby \(x\), then \(R_\lambda(x,\cdot)\) is locally \(\lambda L_p\)-Lipschitz uniformly there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Euclidean parameter set, parameter sensitivity of the forward field transfers to the resolvent residual, with its Lipschitz modulus multiplied by the stepsize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert R_\lambda(x,p)-R_\lambda(x,q)\rVert\le\lambda L_p\lVert p-q\rVert\) locally.

notation.meaning: local parameter Lipschitz modulus of F

children.title: Minimum-Function Equations
children.top_down_role: Complementarity encodings based on componentwise minimum functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Function Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise minimum-function reformulation of nonlinear complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \(\Phi_{\min}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) componentwise by \[\bigl(\Phi_{\min}(x)\bigr)_i:=\min\{x_i,F_i(x)\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\] Then \[\Phi_{\min}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\ge0,\quad F(x)\ge0,\quad x_iF_i(x)=0\ \text{for every }i.\] Thus the nonlinear complementarity problem is exactly equivalent to a generally nonsmooth square equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise minima of each variable and its residual vanish exactly when nonnegativity and complementary orthogonality hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_{\min}(x)=0\iff 0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).

children.title: Maximum-Function Equations
children.top_down_role: Complementarity encodings based on componentwise maximum functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Function Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed componentwise maximum-function reformulation of nonlinear complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \(\Phi_{\max}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) componentwise by \[\bigl(\Phi_{\max}(x)\bigr)_i:=\max\{-x_i,-F_i(x)\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\] Since \(\max\{-a,-b\}=-\min\{a,b\}\), \[\Phi_{\max}(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\ge0,\quad F(x)\ge0,\quad x_iF_i(x)=0\ \text{for every }i.\] Hence this signed maximum equation is equivalent to both the minimum-function equation and the nonlinear complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed componentwise maximum residual is the negative minimum residual and has exactly the complementarity solutions as its zeros.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_{\max}(x)=0\iff 0\le x\perp F(x)\ge0\).

children.title: Active-Piece Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between complementarity states and selected affine pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Piece Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between active extremum pieces and local derivative selections away from ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m(a,b):=\min\{a,b\}\) and \(M(a,b):=\max\{-a,-b\}=-m(a,b)\), the active piece is determined by the ordering of \(a\) and \(b\). If \(a<b\), then locally \(m(a,b)=a\) and \(M(a,b)=-a\); if \(b<a\), then locally \(m(a,b)=b\) and \(M(a,b)=-b\). At a tie \(a=b\), both pieces are active, with Clarke subdifferentials \[\partial m(a,b)=\operatorname{co}\{(1,0),(0,1)\},\qquad \partial M(a,b)=-\partial m(a,b).\] The correspondence applies componentwise to extremum-function complementarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict ordering selects one smooth extremum piece; at a tie both pieces are active and their derivative vectors generate the generalized derivative set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active derivatives are \((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\) off ties, and their convex hull at ties; maximum derivatives have the opposite sign.

children.title: Tie-Point Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Local geometry where multiple minimum or maximum pieces are simultaneously active.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Point Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke local structure of the minimum-function complementarity equation at an active-piece tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be defined by \(m(a,b)=\min\{a,b\}\). If \(a=b\), both smooth pieces are active and
\[
\partial_C m(a,a)=\operatorname{co}\{(1,0),(0,1)\}.
\]
If additionally \(m(a,b)=0\), then \((a,b)=(0,0)\). At this complementary tie, every Clarke generalized-gradient row has the form \((\theta,1-\theta)\) with \(\theta\in[0,1]\), so the active-piece gradient is not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the minimum-function equation, an active-piece tie satisfying the equation occurs only at the origin, where the Clarke generalized gradient is the line segment joining the two piece gradients and hence is nonunique.

children.title: Fischer–Burmeister Equations
children.top_down_role: Standard and modified Fischer–Burmeister residual families.

children.title: Standard Fischer–Burmeister Residuals
children.top_down_role: The basic Fischer–Burmeister equation representation and its local structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Standard Fischer–Burmeister Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard componentwise equation representation of nonnegative complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Fischer–Burmeister function by
\[
\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b.
\]
For \(a,b\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\geq0,\ b\geq0,\ ab=0.
\]
Hence, for \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), the nonlinear complementarity problem \(0\leq x\perp F(x)\geq0\) is equivalent to the nonsmooth equation \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\), where \((\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))_i=\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x_i,F_i(x))\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fischer–Burmeister scalar function vanishes exactly on complementary nonnegative pairs, yielding a componentwise equation equivalent to a nonlinear complementarity problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\iff 0\leq x\perp F(x)\geq0\).

notation.meaning: componentwise orthogonality, here combined with nonnegativity

children.title: Modified Fischer–Burmeister Residuals
children.top_down_role: Penalized, asymmetric, and related Fischer–Burmeister variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Modified Fischer–Burmeister Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A zero-set-preserving weighted and asymmetric Fischer–Burmeister family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha,\beta>0\), and let \(q:\mathbb R^2\to(0,\infty)\) be locally Lipschitz. Define
\[
\psi_{\alpha,\beta,q}(a,b)=q(a,b)\bigl(\sqrt{\alpha^2a^2+\beta^2b^2}-\alpha a-\beta b\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
\psi_{\alpha,\beta,q}(a,b)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\geq0,\ b\geq0,\ ab=0.
\]
Thus replacing each standard Fischer–Burmeister row by \(\psi_{\alpha_i,\beta_i,q_i}(x_i,F_i(x))\) preserves the complementarity solution set while permitting asymmetric scaling and positive residual weighting. Its generalized-derivative structure changes with the selected weights even though its zeros do not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive asymmetric scalings and positive locally Lipschitz weights modify Fischer–Burmeister residuals without changing their complementarity zero set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\psi_{\alpha,\beta,q}(a,b)=0\iff a\geq0,\ b\geq0,\ ab=0\).

children.title: Fischer–Burmeister Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Pointwise, sequential, and Newton-approximation regularity classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Fischer–Burmeister Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise smoothness and generalized-derivative regimes of the scalar Fischer–Burmeister function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\), the function is continuously differentiable on \(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\), with
\[
\nabla\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\left(\frac{a}{r}-1,\frac{b}{r}-1\right),\qquad r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.
\]
It is locally Lipschitz, directionally differentiable, and strongly semismooth on \(\mathbb R^2\). At the unique nonsmooth point,
\[
\partial_C\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(0,0)=\{(u-1,v-1):u^2+v^2\leq1\}.
\]
Accordingly, classical Jacobians apply away from complementary ties, whereas generalized or sequential Jacobian selections are required at a tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fischer–Burmeister function is smooth away from the origin and strongly semismooth everywhere; at the origin its Clarke gradient is a translated unit disk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}\) is \(C^1\) off \((0,0)\), strongly semismooth everywhere, and has the displayed Clarke gradient at \((0,0)\).

children.title: Alternative Complementarity-Function Equations
children.top_down_role: Complementarity encodings distinguished by smoothness, symmetry, and generalized-derivative structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative Complementarity-Function Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar complementarity functions and their componentwise equation encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(\phi:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is a complementarity function if
\[
\phi(a,b)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a\geq0,\ b\geq0,\ ab=0.
\]
Two standard choices are
\[
\phi_{\min}(a,b)=\min\{a,b\},\qquad
\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b.
\]
For any such \(\phi\) and mapping \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), define \(\Phi_i(x)=\phi(x_i,F_i(x))\). Then \(\Phi(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(0\leq x\perp F(x)\geq0\). Different choices preserve the zero set but may differ in symmetry, smoothness, and generalized Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any scalar function whose zeros are precisely complementary nonnegative pairs yields an equivalent componentwise complementarity equation; minimum and Fischer–Burmeister functions are standard choices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(x)=0\iff0\leq x\perp F(x)\geq0\).

children.title: Bounded Complementarity Equation Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Equation formulations for mixed complementarity, finite-bound, and box-constrained systems.

children.title: Mixed Complementarity Systems
children.top_down_role: Equation representations containing free, lower-bounded, upper-bounded, or complementary components.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Complementarity Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise mixed complementarity with finite or infinite variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), and let \(-\infty\leq l_i<u_i\leq+\infty\). A vector \(x\) solves the mixed complementarity problem \(\operatorname{MCP}(F,l,u)\) when, for every \(i\), exactly the applicable bound conditions hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_i=l_i&\ \Longrightarrow\ F_i(x)\geq0,\\
l_i<x_i<u_i&\ \Longrightarrow\ F_i(x)=0,\\
x_i=u_i&\ \Longrightarrow\ F_i(x)\leq0,
\end{aligned}
\]
with equality to an infinite bound excluded. Equivalently, \(l\leq x\leq u\) and \(0\in F(x)+N_{[l,u]}(x)\), using the convex-analytic normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed complementarity solution satisfies a sign condition at each finite active bound and a zero equation for every interior or free variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) solves \(\operatorname{MCP}(F,l,u)\iff0\in F(x)+N_{[l,u]}(x)\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to the bound set

children.title: Finite-Bound Complementarity Systems
children.top_down_role: Residual encodings for components with finite lower or upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Bound Complementarity Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min–max equation representation when every lower and upper bound is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) and \(l,u\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(l_i<u_i\). Define the finite-bound residual componentwise by
\[
R_i(x)=\min\bigl\{x_i-l_i,\ \max\{F_i(x),x_i-u_i\}\bigr\}.
\]
Then \(R(x)=0\) if and only if \(l\leq x\leq u\) and, for every \(i\),
\[
x_i=l_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\geq0,\qquad
l_i<x_i<u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)=0,\qquad
x_i=u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\leq0.
\]
Thus a finite-bound complementarity system is represented by one generally nonsmooth square equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finite bounds, a nested minimum–maximum residual vanishes exactly when all lower-bound, interior, and upper-bound complementarity conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x)=0\) is equivalent to the finite-bound complementarity conditions.

children.title: Box-Constrained Complementarity Systems
children.top_down_role: Equation representations for variables constrained by paired finite bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained Complementarity Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent representations of box variational inequalities through normal-cone inclusions and complementarity signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=[l,u]\subset\mathbb R^n\) with finite \(l_i<u_i\), and let \(F:B\to\mathbb R^n\). For \(x\in B\), the following are equivalent:
\[
\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }y\in B,
\]
\[
0\in F(x)+N_B(x),
\]
and the componentwise conditions
\[
x_i=l_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\geq0,\quad
l_i<x_i<u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)=0,\quad
x_i=u_i\Rightarrow F_i(x)\leq0.
\]
Thus the box-constrained variational inequality, its normal-cone inclusion, and its bounded complementarity system represent the same solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box variational inequality, its normal-cone inclusion, and the corresponding bound-dependent componentwise sign conditions are equivalent representations of the same solution set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VI}(F,B)\), \(0\in F(x)+N_B(x)\), and the displayed complementarity conditions are equivalent.

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to the box

children.title: Bound-Activity Encoding
children.top_down_role: Representation of inactive, lower-active, upper-active, and fixed-variable states.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Activity Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Index-set encoding of lower-active, free, and upper-active complementarity rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible point \(x\in[l,u]\), define
\[
\mathcal L(x)=\{i:x_i=l_i\},\qquad
\mathcal I(x)=\{i:l_i<x_i<u_i\},\qquad
\mathcal U(x)=\{i:x_i=u_i\}.
\]
The bounded complementarity conditions are encoded by
\[
F_i(x)\geq0\ (i\in\mathcal L(x)),\qquad
F_i(x)=0\ (i\in\mathcal I(x)),\qquad
F_i(x)\leq0\ (i\in\mathcal U(x)).
\]
For the min–max residual \(R_i(x)=\min\{x_i-l_i,\max\{F_i(x),x_i-u_i\}\}\), these sets identify the candidate active affine pieces. Coincident piece values create ties and require generalized-Jacobian rather than unique branch selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower-active, interior, and upper-active index sets encode which sign or equality condition—and which local residual piece—applies to each variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) satisfies bounded complementarity exactly when the displayed conditions hold on \(\mathcal L(x),\mathcal I(x),\mathcal U(x)\).

children.title: KKT Residual Systems
children.top_down_role: Primal-dual residual representations of smooth and nonsmooth optimality systems.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Residual Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fischer–Burmeister residual representation of smooth nonlinear-program KKT conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\), and \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, and consider
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\leq0.
\]
For multipliers \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R^m\), define \(L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}h(x)+\mu^{\mathsf T}g(x)\) and
\[
R(x,\lambda,\mu)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\nabla_xL(x,\lambda,\mu)\\
h(x)\\
\bigl(\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(\mu_i,-g_i(x))\bigr)_{i=1}^m
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b.
\]
Then \(R(x,\lambda,\mu)=0\) if and only if stationarity, equality feasibility, dual feasibility \(\mu\geq0\), inequality feasibility \(g(x)\leq0\), and complementary slackness \(\mu_i g_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) all hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional smooth nonlinear program, stationarity, equality feasibility, and inequality complementarity form one square residual system through componentwise Fischer–Burmeister equations.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\), and \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) are continuously differentiable
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x,\lambda,\mu)=0\) is equivalent to the displayed KKT system.

notation.meaning: square primal-dual KKT residual mapping into \(\mathbb R^{n+p+m}\)

children.title: Composite Stationarity Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual targets for composite and proximal stationarity systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Stationarity Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient residual for smooth-plus-convex composite stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, let \(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and choose \(\gamma>0\). Define
\[
R_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
R_\gamma(x)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x).
\]
Thus zeros of the proximal-gradient residual are exactly stationary points of the composite objective \(f+g\). The unscaled displacement \(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\) has the same zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal-gradient mapping vanishes exactly when the smooth-plus-convex composite stationarity inclusion holds.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\gamma(x)=0\iff0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\).

notation.meaning: proximal mapping of the scaled function

children.title: Generalized-Equation Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Set-valued targets with separately linearizable single-valued and multifunction components.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Equation Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued equation target and its affine single-valued local model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional normed spaces, let \(f:X\to Y\) be single-valued, and let \(Q:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be set-valued. The generalized equation is
\[
0\in f(x)+Q(x).
\]
At an iterate \(x_k\), given a linear approximation \(A_k:X\to Y\) to \(f\), its Newton-type local model seeks a step \(d_k\) satisfying
\[
0\in f(x_k)+A_kd_k+Q(x_k+d_k).
\]
The single-valued term is affine-linearized while the multifunction is retained at the trial point. If a solution step exists, the next iterate is \(x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized equation combines a single-valued mapping with a multifunction; its Newton model linearizes the former while retaining the latter at the trial point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local Newton target is \(0\in f(x_k)+A_kd_k+Q(x_k+d_k)\).

notation.meaning: linear local approximation of the single-valued term

children.title: Mixed Variational-Equation Systems
children.top_down_role: Coupled systems combining equations, variational inequalities, and multiplier blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Variational-Equation Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coupled equation, variational-inequality, and multiplier representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) and \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be nonempty closed convex sets. A mixed variational-equation system seeks \((x,u,\lambda)\in\mathbb R^n\times C\times K\) satisfying
\[
H(x,u,\lambda)=0,\qquad 0\in G(x,u,\lambda)+N_C(u),\qquad 0\in q(x,u)+N_K(\lambda).
\]
Equivalently, the middle block is the variational inequality
\[
\langle G(x,u,\lambda),v-u\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }v\in C.
\]
Thus the entire system is the generalized equation \(0\in\mathcal F(x,u,\lambda)+\{0\}\times N_C(u)\times N_K(\lambda)\), where \(\mathcal F=(H,G,q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed system combines a smooth or nonsmooth equation block with variational-inequality and multiplier normal-cone inclusions in one generalized equation.
assumptions_latex: \(H,G,q\) are single-valued maps of compatible finite dimensions.
\(C\) and \(K\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\mathcal F(x,u,\lambda)+\{0\}\times N_C(u)\times N_K(\lambda)\) represents all coupled blocks.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to C at u.

children.title: Reformulation Fidelity Principle

children.title: Solution-Set Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Global and localized correspondence between original systems and equation targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global correspondence and its localization near a reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the original system have solution set \(S\subseteq X\), and let its equation reformulation be \(R(z)=0\) on \(Z\). A map \(E:X\to Z\) gives exact solution-set correspondence when
\[
x\in S\quad\Longleftrightarrow
 R(E(x))=0,
\qquad
E(S)=R^{-1}(0),
\]
and \(E|_S\) is bijective. At \(\bar x	ext{ in }S\), with \(\bar z=E(\bar x)\), local correspondence means that neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar z\) exist such that \(E\) bijects \(S\cap U\) onto \(R^{-1}(0)\cap V\). If the restricted maps are homeomorphisms, convergence to corresponding solutions is preserved locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A faithful reformulation bijectively matches original solutions and equation roots, globally or within neighborhoods of corresponding reference solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(E:X\to Z\) is the encoding used by the reformulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(S)=R^{-1}(0)\), globally or after restriction to corresponding neighborhoods.

notation.meaning: Solution set of the original system.
Root set of the reformulated residual.

children.title: Regularity Transfer Between Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Transfer of inverse stability and generalized-derivative regularity between representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity Transfer Between Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer under invertible linear changes of variables and residual coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\), let \(A,B\) be invertible linear maps, and define \(G(y)=AF(By)\). If \(F(\bar x)=0\) and \(\bar y=B^{-1}\bar x\), then \(G(\bar y)=0\), and
\[
G^{-1}(v)=B^{-1}F^{-1}(A^{-1}v).
\]
Consequently, \(F^{-1}\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization at \((0,\bar x)\) if and only if \(G^{-1}\) has one at \((0,\bar y)\). Moreover, if \(\operatorname{lip}F^{-1}(0\mid\bar x)=\kappa\), then
\[
\operatorname{lip}G^{-1}(0\mid\bar y)\leq \lVert B^{-1}\rVert\,\kappa\,\lVert A^{-1}\rVert.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong metric regularity is invariant under invertible linear variable and residual transformations, while its Lipschitz modulus changes by operator-norm factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong metric regularity of \(F\) and \(G=AFB\) is equivalent, with the displayed modulus bound.

notation.meaning: Exact local Lipschitz modulus of the localized inverse.

children.title: Residual Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity properties associated with the chosen residual representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local error-bound conditioning of an equation residual at a root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), and let \(\bar x\in S\). The local residual-conditioning modulus of \(F\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\kappa_F(\bar x):=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}
\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}{\lVert F(x)\rVert},
\]
where the value is defined to be \(0\) if no points of \(\mathbb R^n\setminus S\) occur arbitrarily close to \(\bar x\), and is \(+\infty\) when the quotient is locally unbounded. Finite residual conditioning is equivalent to a local error bound: there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a finite constant \(\kappa\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa\lVert F(x)\rVert
\quad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
The infimum of all constants admissible in such local error bounds equals \(\kappa_F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual conditioning is the exact local modulus, defined as the infimum of factors that convert residual norm into distance to the equation's root set.
assumptions_latex: Fixed norms are used on the domain and residual spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_F(\bar x)<+\infty\) exactly when a local error bound of the displayed form holds.

children.title: Variable Scaling Effects
children.top_down_role: Changes in local equation geometry caused by rescaling variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Scaling Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of an invertible variable transformation on local residual conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be invertible, define \(G(z)=F(Sz)\), and set \(\bar z=S^{-1}\bar x\). Then \(G^{-1}(0)=S^{-1}F^{-1}(0)\). With induced operator norms, the local conditioning moduli satisfy
\[
\frac{1}{\lVert S\rVert}\,\kappa_F(\bar x)
\leq \kappa_G(\bar z)
\leq \lVert S^{-1}\rVert\,\kappa_F(\bar x).
\]
Thus an invertible variable scaling preserves finiteness of the local error-bound modulus but may multiply its numerical value by factors controlled by \(S\). In particular, a poorly conditioned variable transformation can make an otherwise well-conditioned residual appear ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible variable scaling preserves roots and finite error bounds, but changes conditioning by factors bounded through the scaling operator and its inverse.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\bar x)=0\) and \(\kappa_F(\bar x)\) is measured in fixed norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert S\rVert^{-1}\kappa_F(\bar x)\leq\kappa_G(\bar z)\leq\lVert S^{-1}\rVert\kappa_F(\bar x)\).

children.title: Equation Scaling Effects

knowledge_statements.title: Equation Scaling Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of invertible residual-space scaling on local error-bound conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m\) be invertible and define \(G(x)=TF(x)\). Then \(G^{-1}(0)=F^{-1}(0)\). For every \(x\),
\[
\lVert T^{-1}\rVert^{-1}\lVert F(x)\rVert
\leq \lVert G(x)\rVert
\leq \lVert T\rVert\lVert F(x)\rVert.
\]
Consequently, at every root \(\bar x\),
\[
\frac{1}{\lVert T\rVert}\,\kappa_F(\bar x)
\leq \kappa_G(\bar x)
\leq \lVert T^{-1}\rVert\,\kappa_F(\bar x).
\]
Equation scaling therefore preserves the root set and finiteness of residual conditioning, but changes the numerical modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible equation scaling leaves the root set unchanged while altering residual conditioning according to the scaling operator’s norm and inverse norm.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\bar x)=0\) and fixed norms define both conditioning moduli.
\(T\) is an invertible linear residual-space map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert T\rVert^{-1}\kappa_F(\bar x)\leq\kappa_G(\bar x)\leq\lVert T^{-1}\rVert\kappa_F(\bar x)\).

children.title: Norm-Dependent Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of conditioning assessments on domain and residual norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Dependent Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of numerical sensitivity moduli on equivalent finite-dimensional norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose domain norms \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{X,1},\lVert\cdot\rVert_{X,2}\) and residual norms \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{Y,1},\lVert\cdot\rVert_{Y,2}\) satisfy
\[
a_X\lVert h\rVert_{X,1}\leq\lVert h\rVert_{X,2}\leq b_X\lVert h\rVert_{X,1},
\quad
a_Y\lVert r\rVert_{Y,1}\leq\lVert r\rVert_{Y,2}\leq b_Y\lVert r\rVert_{Y,1}.
\]
For the corresponding residual-conditioning moduli at a root \(\bar x\),
\[
\frac{a_X}{b_Y}\kappa_1(\bar x)
\leq\kappa_2(\bar x)
\leq\frac{b_X}{a_Y}\kappa_1(\bar x).
\]
Hence finiteness of conditioning is norm invariant in finite dimensions, whereas its numerical value is norm dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent finite-dimensional norms preserve whether sensitivity is finite, but rescale its numerical modulus by their equivalence constants.
assumptions_latex: Two equivalent norms are fixed on each finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((a_X/b_Y)\kappa_1(\bar x)\leq\kappa_2(\bar x)\leq(b_X/a_Y)\kappa_1(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Conditioning modulus computed with the ith pair of norms.

children.title: Reformulation-Induced Stationarity Failures
children.top_down_role: Nonroot stationary points and other losses introduced by scalar or equation reformulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation-Induced Stationarity Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth least-squares reformulation with a stationary nonroot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the scalar equation \(F(x)=x^2-1=0\) and its least-squares merit function
\[
\psi(x)=\frac12\lvert F(x)\rvert^2=\frac12(x^2-1)^2.
\]
Its derivative is \(\psi'(x)=2x(x^2-1)\). Therefore \(x=0\) is stationary for the reformulated minimization problem, since \(\psi'(0)=0\), but it is not an equation root because \(F(0)=-1\). Here the failure is enabled by \(F'(0)=0\). More generally, the stationarity equation \(F'(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)=0\) need not imply \(F(x)=0\); it does imply \(F(x)=0\) when \(F'(x)\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring an equation residual can create stationary points that are not roots when the residual derivative loses rank; full row rank excludes this failure at the point under consideration.

knowledge_statements.title: Locally Lipschitz Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local Lipschitz regularity near a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A map \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a constant \(L<+\infty\) such that
\[
\lVert F(x)-F(y)\rVert\leq L\lVert x-y\rVert
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in U.
\]
It is locally Lipschitz on an open set \(\Omega\) if it is locally Lipschitz at every point of \(\Omega\). In finite dimensions, such a map is differentiable almost everywhere; hence its limiting Jacobians and Clarke generalized Jacobian can be constructed from limits and convex hulls of nearby classical Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz residual changes at most linearly with nearby variables and is classically differentiable almost everywhere in finite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: Fixed norms are used on both finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert F(x)-F(y)\rVert\leq L\lVert x-y\rVert\) locally around \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Neighborhood on which the Lipschitz inequality holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitzness and Clarke generalized-Jacobian regularity of a vector map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties of a vector-valued map assembled from locally Lipschitz scalar components and of its Clarke generalized Jacobian at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $h_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, $i=1,\ldots,m$, be locally Lipschitz in a neighborhood of $x$ with constants $K_i$, and define $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_m)^T$. Then $h$ is locally Lipschitz at $x$ with constant $K=\|(K_1,\ldots,K_m)^T\|$; the Clarke generalized Jacobian $\partial h(x)$ is a nonempty, convex, compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$; and the mapping $y\mapsto\partial h(y)$ is upper semicontinuous at $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all scalar components of a vector-valued map are locally Lipschitz near a point, the vector map is locally Lipschitz there with the norm of the component constants. Its Clarke generalized Jacobian at that point is nonempty, convex, and compact, and the generalized-Jacobian mapping is upper semicontinuous at that point.
assumptions_latex: h_i\text{ is locally Lipschitz in a neighborhood of }x\text{ with constant }K_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\text{ is locally Lipschitz at }x\text{ with }K=\|(K_1,\ldots,K_m)^T\|;\quad \partial h(x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\text{ is nonempty, convex, and compact; and }y\mapsto\partial h(y)\text{ is upper semicontinuous at }x.

children.title: Directionally Differentiable Residual Maps
children.top_down_role: Maps possessing directional first-order behavior without necessarily uniform local approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Directionally Differentiable Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional differentiability without a uniform first-order remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A map \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\) if, for every direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), the finite limit
\[
F'(\bar x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{F(\bar x+td)-F(\bar x)}{t}
\]
exists. The resulting map \(d\mapsto F'(\bar x;d)\) is positively homogeneous whenever it is defined. Directional differentiability alone requires neither linearity of this map nor a remainder estimate uniform over varying directions. Hadamard directional differentiability strengthens the definition by requiring the same limit whenever \(t\downarrow0\) and \(d'\to d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional differentiability requires a one-sided first-order limit in every fixed direction, without necessarily giving a uniform local approximation.
assumptions_latex: The directional limit is taken with \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F'(\bar x;d)\) exists finitely for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: One-sided directional derivative at the reference point in direction d.

knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand-Differentiable Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bouligand differentiability via the directional derivative as a uniform first-order model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A map \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there, the map \(d\mapsto F'(\bar x;d)\) is continuous, and
\[
F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-F'(\bar x;h)=o(\lVert h\rVert)
\quad\text{as }h\to0.
\]
The positively homogeneous map \(F'(\bar x;\cdot)\) is then the Bouligand first-order model. Unlike ordinary Fréchet differentiability, this model need not be linear; unlike directional differentiability alone, it approximates increments uniformly to first order as the direction varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability means the continuous directional derivative supplies a possibly nonlinear, positively homogeneous, uniformly accurate first-order model.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x+h)=F(\bar x)+F'(\bar x;h)+o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: Remainder whose norm divided by the norm of h tends to zero.

children.title: Newton-Differentiable Maps

knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Differentiable Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton differentiability defined by an evaluation-shifted linear approximation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), with \(\Omega\) open. A matrix-valued map \(D_NF:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is a Newton derivative of \(F\) at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) if
\[
F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-D_NF(\bar x+h)h=o(\lVert h\rVert)
\quad\text{as }h\to0.
\]
The map \(F\) is Newton differentiable at \(\bar x\) when such a selection exists. More generally, for a set-valued approximation family \(\mathcal D(x)\), the requirement is imposed uniformly over all \(V\in\mathcal D(\bar x+h)\). The derivative is evaluated at the trial point, distinguishing this model from a fixed Fréchet derivative at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton differentiability uses matrices selected at the perturbed point to approximate residual increments with a little-o first-order error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-D_NF(\bar x+h)h=o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: A selected Newton-derivative matrix at x.
Optional set-valued family of admissible approximation matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Slant-Differentiable Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise slant differentiability between finite-dimensional normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\), where \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, and let \(\bar x\in U\). The map \(F\) is slant differentiable at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(V\subseteq U\) of \(\bar x\) and a mapping \(G:V\to\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) such that \[F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-G(\bar x+h)h=o(\lVert h\rVert)\quad\text{as }h\to0.\] The mapping \(G\) is called a slanting function for \(F\) at \(\bar x\). No convergence of \(G(\bar x+h)\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map is slant differentiable when some matrix-valued selection evaluated at the perturbed point gives a first-order model with a little-o residual.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(\bar x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-G(\bar x+h)h=o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: A residual whose norm divided by the step norm tends to zero.

children.title: Approximation-Family Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Family Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between set-valued Newton models and their admissible single-valued slant selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(\bar x\in U\), and let \(\mathcal A:U\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have nonempty values near \(\bar x\). The family \(\mathcal A\) has the uniform Newton approximation property at \(\bar x\) precisely when \[\sup_{A\in\mathcal A(\bar x+h)}\frac{\lVert F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Ah\rVert}{\lVert h\rVert}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }h\to0,\ h\ne0.\] This is equivalent to the slant estimate holding for every selection \(G\) defined near \(\bar x\) and satisfying \(G(x)\in\mathcal A(x)\). Existence of only one such selection corresponds instead to a selection-dependent model property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued approximation family is uniformly Newton accurate exactly when every admissible matrix selection defined near the reference point is an accurate slanting function.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\), and \(\bar x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The uniform family estimate is equivalent to the slant estimate for every selection \(G(x)\in\mathcal A(x)\) defined near \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Set-valued family of candidate linear models.
A single-valued selection from the approximation family.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Dependent Approximation Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes existential slant accuracy from uniform accuracy over an approximation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) and let \(\mathcal A(x)\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be nonempty near \(\bar x\). The existence of a selection \(G(x)\in\mathcal A(x)\) satisfying \[F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-G(\bar x+h)h=o(\lVert h\rVert)\] does not imply the same estimate for every selection. Uniform selection-independent quality requires \[\sup_{A\in\mathcal A(\bar x+h)}\lVert F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Ah\rVert=o(\lVert h\rVert).\] Thus enlarging an approximation family can preserve an accurate selection while destroying its uniform Newton-model property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One accurate matrix selection does not make every selection accurate; selection-independent quality requires a uniform residual bound over the entire family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existential slant accuracy is weaker than uniform accuracy over \(\mathcal A(\bar x+h)\).

notation.meaning: Candidate matrix family at the point.
An admissible selection from that family.

knowledge_statements.title: Semismooth Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke-Jacobian definition for locally Lipschitz finite-dimensional residual maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) be locally Lipschitz on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\bar x\in U\). The residual map \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and \[\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}\lVert F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\rVert=o(\lVert h\rVert)\quad\text{as }h\to0.\] Equivalently, the displayed estimate holds along every sequence \(h_k\to0\) and every choice \(V_k\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz residual is semismooth at the reference point when it is directionally differentiable there and every nearby Clarke generalized Jacobian gives a first-order model with a little-o error.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(\bar x\in U\).
\(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}\lVert F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\rVert=o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of the locally Lipschitz map.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Semismooth Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-remainder strengthening of Clarke semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) be locally Lipschitz on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\bar x\in U\). The map \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and \[\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}\lVert F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\rVert=O(\lVert h\rVert^2)\quad\text{as }h\to0.\] Strong semismoothness implies semismoothness at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz map is strongly semismooth at the reference point when it is directionally differentiable there and every nearby Clarke linearization has a quadratic residual.
assumptions_latex: \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized-Jacobian residual is \(O(\lVert h\rVert^2)\), hence \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: A residual bounded by a constant times the squared step norm locally.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Semismooth Residual Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder-order scale interpolating semismooth and strongly semismooth residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). A locally Lipschitz map \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is semismooth of order \(\alpha\) at \(\bar x\in U\) if it is directionally differentiable there and \[\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}\lVert F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\rVert=O(\lVert h\rVert^{1+\alpha})\quad\text{as }h\to0.\] Order \(\alpha=1\) is strong semismoothness. Every positive order implies ordinary semismoothness, while ordinary semismoothness need not possess a positive power rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz map is semismooth of order alpha at the reference point when it is directionally differentiable there and every nearby generalized-Jacobian model has a residual of order one plus alpha; alpha equal to one recovers strong semismoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and directionally differentiable there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual is \(O(\lVert h\rVert^{1+\alpha})\); for \(\alpha=1\) this is strong semismoothness.

children.title: SC1 Maps

knowledge_statements.title: SC1 Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The finite-dimensional SC1 class defined through semismoothness of the classical derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open. A mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is of class \(SC^1\) on \(U\) if \(F\) is continuously differentiable and its derivative mapping \[DF:U\to\mathbb R^{m\times n}\] is semismooth, with the matrix space equipped with any fixed norm. Pointwise \(SC^1\) at \(\bar x\) means that \(DF\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\). Thus the nonsmooth structure occurs at the derivative level even though \(F\) itself is classically continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SC1 map is continuously differentiable and has a derivative mapping that is itself semismooth as a matrix-valued map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in SC^1(U)\) exactly when \(DF\) is semismooth on \(U\).

notation.meaning: Classical derivative matrix of the continuously differentiable map.
Continuously differentiable with semismooth derivative mapping.

knowledge_statements.title: PC1 Map Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-selection definition of continuous piecewise continuously differentiable maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open. A continuous map \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is piecewise \(C^1\), abbreviated \(PC^1\), if there exist finitely many maps \(F_i:U\to\mathbb R^m\) of class \(C^1\) such that \[F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_N(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The active index set is \[I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}:F(x)=F_i(x)\}.\] The maps \(F_i\) are selection functions; their domains need not form a disjoint partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PC1 map is continuous and, at every point, equals one of finitely many continuously differentiable selection functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are finitely many \(C^1\) selections \(F_i\) with \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_N(x)\}\) for all \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: Smooth selection functions representing the piecewise map.
Indices of selections agreeing with the map at the point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting Jacobian Formula for a PC1 Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-Jacobian structure of a PC1 map and its directional-derivative model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let G be \mathrm{PC}^{1} on a neighborhood \mathcal N of x with C^{1} pieces \{G^{i}:i\in\mathcal K\}, where \mathcal K=\{1,\ldots,k\}. Define
\[
\widetilde{\mathcal P}(x):=\left\{i:x\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{int}\{z\in\mathcal N:i\in\mathcal P(z)\}\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Jac}(G'(x;\cdot),0)\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(G,x)=\{JG^{i}(x):i\in\widetilde{\mathcal P}(x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a PC1 map, the limiting Jacobian at x consists exactly of the Jacobians of pieces whose activity regions have x in the closure of their interiors. The limiting Jacobian at zero of the directional-derivative map is contained in that set.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is }\mathrm{PC}^{1}\text{ on a neighborhood }\mathcal N\text{ of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Jac}(G'(x;\cdot),0)\subseteq\operatorname{Jac}(G,x)=\{JG^{i}(x):i\in\widetilde{\mathcal P}(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a \mathrm{PC}^{1} map near x with C^{1} pieces \{G^{1},\ldots,G^{k}\}. Then G is B-differentiable at every point near x, and G'(x;\cdot) is piecewise linear with linear pieces drawn from \{JG^{1}(x),\ldots,JG^{k}(x)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PC1 map is B-differentiable at every nearby point. At the reference point, its directional derivative is piecewise linear, with linear pieces among the Jacobians of its smooth pieces at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is B-differentiable at every point near }x,\qquad G'(x;\cdot)\text{ is piecewise linear with pieces drawn from }\{JG^{i}(x)\}_{i=1}^{k}.

children.title: General Piecewise-Smooth Maps
children.top_down_role: Residual maps assembled from locally selected smooth pieces beyond the PC1 regime.

knowledge_statements.title: General Piecewise-Smooth Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally finite smooth-piece representation without a globally finite selection list.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open. A continuous map \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally piecewise smooth if every \(\bar x\in U\) has a neighborhood \(V\) and finitely many smooth maps \(F_1,\ldots,F_N:V\to\mathbb R^m\) such that \[F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_N(x)\}\quad\text{for all }x\in V.\] The number and identities of the selections may vary with \(V\). Replacing “smooth” by \(C^r\) defines the locally piecewise-\(C^r\) class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generally piecewise-smooth map has a finite smooth selection representation around each point, although no single finite family need work globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point has a neighborhood on which \(F\) is represented by finitely many smooth selections.

notation.meaning: A neighborhood carrying a finite local representation.

children.title: Smooth-Piece Atlases
children.top_down_role: Local collections of smooth pieces and their associated selection regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-Piece Atlases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atlas representation of a map by compatible locally finite smooth pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth-piece atlas for \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is a locally finite family \(\{(U_i,F_i)\}_{i\in I}\), where each \(U_i\subseteq U\) is relatively closed, the sets cover \(U\), and each \(F_i\) extends smoothly to a neighborhood of \(U_i\). It represents \(F\) when \[F(x)=F_i(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in U_i,\] with compatibility \[F_i(x)=F_j(x)\quad\text{for }x\in U_i\cap U_j.\] Local finiteness means every point has a neighborhood intersecting only finitely many pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth-piece atlas covers the domain by locally finite closed pieces carrying compatible smooth formulas that agree with the represented map.
assumptions_latex: \(\{U_i\}_{i\in I}\) is a locally finite cover of \(U\) by relatively closed sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatible smooth extensions \(F_i\) satisfying \(F|_{U_i}=F_i|_{U_i}\) constitute a smooth-piece representation of \(F\).

notation.meaning: A domain piece in the atlas.
A smooth formula extending beyond its piece.

children.title: Local-Finiteness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limitations arising when a locally finite smooth-piece representation is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Finiteness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite active-piece calculus when infinitely many pieces accumulate locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Local finiteness cannot be omitted from a smooth-piece atlas if finite active-piece formulas are intended. For example, set \(x_k=1/k\), prescribe \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x_k)=x_k^2\), and make \(f\) affine on every interval \([x_{k+1},x_k]\). Then infinitely many affine pieces and their distinct junctions accumulate at \(0\). Consequently, this displayed piece decomposition is not locally finite at \(0\), and no neighborhood of \(0\) permits its active-piece data to be reduced to finitely many members of that decomposition. Calculus rules requiring a finite local active set therefore do not apply to this atlas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If infinitely many smooth pieces accumulate at a point, that atlas has no finite local active set, so finite-piece calculus cannot be invoked there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine-piece decomposition is not locally finite at \(0\), so finite active-piece rules are unavailable for that decomposition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example plausibly demonstrates failure of local finiteness for the displayed decomposition, but the record supplies no citation for either the counterexample or the boundary imposed on finite active-piece calculus.

children.title: Piecewise-Affine Maps
children.top_down_role: Maps admitting finitely many exact affine local models.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral representation by exact affine formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is piecewise affine if there exist finitely many polyhedral sets \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\) whose union is \(\mathbb R^n\), matrices \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and vectors \(b_i\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \[F(x)=A_i x+b_i\quad\text{whenever }x\in P_i.\] On overlaps, the affine formulas must agree wherever \(F\) is single-valued. A local version requires such a finite polyhedral representation only on a neighborhood of each point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-affine map equals one of finitely many compatible affine formulas on a finite polyhedral cover of its domain.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are polyhedral and cover \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F|_{P_i}(x)=A_i x+b_i\) for every piece \(P_i\), with compatible values on overlaps.

notation.meaning: Polyhedral region of an affine formula.
Affine selection on the corresponding region.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Range, Fibers, and Global Lipschitz Continuity of Piecewise-Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global geometric and continuity properties; the source's fiber quantifier is dimensionally corrected to range over the codomain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be piecewise affine. Then \(\operatorname{range}\Phi\) is a finite union of polyhedra and hence closed. For every \(q\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(\Phi^{-1}(q)\) is a finite union of polyhedra and hence closed; in particular, \(\Phi^{-1}(0)\) is piecewise polyhedral. Moreover, \(\Phi\) is globally Lipschitz continuous on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-affine map has a closed finite-polyhedral-union range and closed finite-polyhedral-union fibers; its zero set is piecewise polyhedral, and the map is globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{range}\Phi\text{ and every }\Phi^{-1}(q),\ q\in\mathbb{R}^m,\text{ are closed finite unions of polyhedra},\quad\Phi^{-1}(0)\text{ is piecewise polyhedral},\quad\Phi\text{ is globally Lipschitz}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proximal mapping \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(z):=\mathop{\rm argmin}_{x}\{f(x)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|x-z\|^2\}\) is single-valued and piecewise affine on a finite polyhedral subdivision of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The projection \(P_C=\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_C}\) has the same structure. Consequently, finite affine compositions and residuals such as \(R(z):=z-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(z)\) and \(G(x):=x-P_C(x-H(x))\), with piecewise-affine \(H\), are piecewise affine. Each such map is globally Lipschitz when its finitely many affine pieces have globally bounded linear parts, and is locally Lipschitz in every case covered by a finite local subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex PLQ proximal maps and polyhedral projections are piecewise affine; affine compositions and their stationarity residuals inherit this local model structure.

children.title: Switching Regions
children.top_down_role: Regions where a single smooth or affine piece determines the residual map.

knowledge_statements.title: Switching Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Region geometry for a finite piecewise-smooth representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A switching-region representation of \(F\) is a finite family \(\{R_i\}_{i=1}^p\) of sets closed relative to \(U\) that covers \(U\), together with maps \(F_i:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\), such that \(F(x)=F_i(x)\) for every \(x\in R_i\). Define the open region \(\Omega_i:=\operatorname{int}_U R_i\) and the switching locus \(\Sigma:=U\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^p\Omega_i\). Then \(\Sigma\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^p\partial_U R_i\). At every \(x\in U\setminus\Sigma\), at least one fixed piece represents \(F\) throughout a neighborhood of \(x\); the representation need not be unique when regions overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switching regions are the interiors, relative to the domain, of closed sets carrying fixed smooth formulas. Outside the switching locus at least one formula remains valid on a neighborhood, although overlapping regions may provide more than one.
assumptions_latex: The sets \(R_i\subset U\) are closed relative to \(U\), and \(U=\bigcup_{i=1}^pR_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(\Omega_i:=\operatorname{int}_U R_i\), switching can occur only on \(\Sigma:=U\setminus\bigcup_i\Omega_i\subseteq\bigcup_i\partial_U R_i\).

notation.meaning: Closed region on which the ith smooth piece represents the map
Interior of the ith region relative to U
Boundary of the ith region relative to U
Switching locus not covered by any region interior

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the active set by \(I(x):=\{i:\phi_i(x)=a(x)\}\). For distinct indices \(i\) and \(j\), their tie set is \(T_{ij}:=\{x\in U:i,j\in I(x)\}=\{x\in U:\phi_i(x)=\phi_j(x)=a(x)\}\). The total tie set is \(T:=\bigcup_{1\leq i<j\leq p}T_{ij}=\{x\in U:|I(x)|\geq2\}\). Thus a point belongs to \(T\) exactly when the selected value admits at least two generating pieces. For maximum or minimum aggregation, the equality with \(a(x)\) additionally enforces extremality among all pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tie set consists of points where two or more generating pieces simultaneously equal the selected aggregate value.

children.title: Switching-Set Incidence
children.top_down_role: Local adjacency and intersection patterns among active-piece regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Switching-Set Incidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial encoding of local tie-set intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The switching-set incidence family at \(x\) is \(\mathcal{E}(x):=\{\{i,j\}:1\leq i<j\leq p,\ x\in T_{ij}\}\). It satisfies \(\mathcal{E}(x)=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in I(x),\ i<j\}\), so the incident pairwise tie sets form the edge set of the complete graph on \(I(x)\). For every \(J\subseteq I(x)\) with \(|J|\geq2\), define \(T_J:=\bigcap_{i,j\in J,\ i<j}T_{ij}\); then \(x\in T_J\). Thus \(I(x)\) determines every pairwise and higher-order incidence. Conversely, when \(|I(x)|\geq2\), the vertices appearing in \(\mathcal{E}(x)\) recover \(I(x)\); when \(|I(x)|=1\), \(\mathcal{E}(x)=\varnothing\) does not identify the unique active index.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The active set determines all incident pairwise tie sets. At a multiple tie the incident edges also recover the active indices, whereas an empty edge family cannot distinguish different singleton active sets.
assumptions_latex: The pairwise tie sets \(T_{ij}\) arise from a finite selection with active set \(I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active set \(I(x)\) determines \(\mathcal{E}(x)\); the converse holds from incidence data when \(|I(x)|\geq2\), but not when \(|I(x)|=1\).

notation.meaning: Incident pairwise tie sets at the point
Higher-order incidence stratum for an index set of cardinality at least two

children.title: Tie-Induced Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Loss of model uniqueness or regularity at multi-piece intersections.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Induced Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LICQ-type degeneracy of a multiple smooth tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Enumerate \(I(\bar x)\setminus\{i_0\}=\{i_1,\ldots,i_{q-1}\}\) and define \(g(x):=(\phi_{i_1}(x)-\phi_{i_0}(x),\ldots,\phi_{i_{q-1}}(x)-\phi_{i_0}(x))\). The active tie is nondegenerate when the gradients \(\{\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)-\nabla\phi_{i_0}(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\setminus\{i_0\}\}\) are linearly independent, equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}Dg(\bar x)=q-1\). It is tie-induced degenerate when this rank condition fails. Nondegeneracy makes the active equality locus \(g^{-1}(0)\) a local smooth manifold of codimension \(q-1\); degeneracy removes that regular-manifold conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple tie is degenerate when its active pairwise equality gradients are linearly dependent, so the expected smooth tie stratum need not exist.
assumptions_latex: The active generators \(\phi_i\) are continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
A reference index \(i_0\in I(\bar x)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tie at \(\bar x\) is nondegenerate exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}Dg(\bar x)=q-1\); otherwise it is tie-induced degenerate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The composition \(F:=G\circ H\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\). Its Clarke generalized Jacobian satisfies \(\partial_C F(\bar x)\subseteq\{DG(H(\bar x))A:A\in\partial_C H(\bar x)\}\). If instead the inner map \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) is continuously differentiable and the outer map \(K:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is locally Lipschitz, then \(\partial_C(K\circ g)(\bar x)\subseteq\{B Dg(\bar x):B\in\partial_C K(g(\bar x))\}\). These inclusions provide compatible local linear models; equality requires additional regularity and is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth Jacobian multiplies the generalized Jacobians of the nonsmooth factor, yielding chain-rule inclusions for either composition order.

children.title: Maximum Aggregation Maps
children.top_down_role: Finite maximum constructions with active-index structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Aggregation Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maxima of continuously differentiable scalar functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), define \(m(x):=\max_{1\leq i\leq p}\phi_i(x)\), and define \(I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\phi_i(x)=m(x)\}\). Then \(m\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable. For every \(x\in U\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(m'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\nabla\phi_i(x)^\top d\). Moreover, \(m\) is Clarke regular and \(\partial_Cm(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla\phi_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\). Thus only active generators contribute to these first-order local models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite smooth maximum has directional derivative equal to the maximum active directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential equal to the convex hull of the active gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in U\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(m'(x;d)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\nabla\phi_i(x)^\top d\) and \(\partial_Cm(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla\phi_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Aggregation Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite minima of continuously differentiable scalar functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), define \(q(x):=\min_{1\leq i\leq p}\phi_i(x)\), and define \(I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\phi_i(x)=q(x)\}\). Then \(q\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable. For every \(x\in U\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(q'(x;d)=\min_{i\in I(x)}\nabla\phi_i(x)^\top d\), and \(\partial_Cq(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla\phi_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\). Unlike a finite maximum, a finite minimum need not be Clarke regular, so its ordinary directional derivative can differ from its Clarke generalized directional derivative at a tie.

children.title: Finite Selection Maps
children.top_down_role: Maps formed by choosing among finitely many local selection functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Selection Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous vector-valued selections from finitely many smooth maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb{N}\). The map \(F\) is a finite selection of \(F_1,\ldots,F_p\) when \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_p(x)\}\) for every \(x\in U\). Define \(I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:F(x)=F_i(x)\}\). Continuity of \(F\), finiteness of the family, and continuous differentiability of the pieces imply that \(F\) is locally Lipschitz. For every \(x\in U\), \(\partial_CF(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{DF_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\). Equality is not automatic because an index can be active at \(x\) without its piece being realized arbitrarily near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous finite selection chooses among finitely many smooth vector maps, is locally Lipschitz, and has a Clarke generalized Jacobian contained in the convex hull of its active piece Jacobians.
assumptions_latex: \(F:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuous and satisfies \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_p(x)\}\) for every \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(F\) is locally Lipschitz and, for every \(x\in U\), satisfies \(\partial_CF(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{DF_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\).

children.top_down_role: Consistency of active indices across components, blocks, or nested selections.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the directionally realizable active set by \(I(x;d):=\{i:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ F(x+t_kd_k)=F_i(x+t_kd_k)\}\). Active-index compatibility in direction \(d\) is the condition \(DF_i(x)d=DF_j(x)d\) for every \(i,j\in I(x;d)\). Under this condition, all selection sequences approaching \(x\) in direction \(d\) yield the same first-order value, and \(F'(x;d)=DF_i(x)d\) for any \(i\in I(x;d)\). Compatibility for every direction gives a well-defined directional local model, although it does not require the full Jacobians \(DF_i(x)\) to coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directionally realizable active pieces are compatible when their Jacobians act identically on that direction, making the selection's directional derivative unambiguous.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Index Compatibility

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z:=g(\bar x)\), \(y:=P_C(z)\), and \(K:=T_C(y)\cap(z-y)^\perp\). The polyhedral projection is piecewise affine and directionally differentiable, with \(P_C'(z;h)=P_K(h)\) for every \(h\in\mathbb{R}^p\). Therefore the composition \(F:=P_C\circ g\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\), and its directional local model is \(F'(\bar x;d)=P_K(Dg(\bar x)d)\). At differentiability points of the projection, the ordinary chain rule gives \(DF(\bar x)=DP_C(z)Dg(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth map followed by polyhedral projection has a directional derivative obtained by projecting the inner linearization onto the associated critical cone.
