children.title: Near-Singularity Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundary behavior between uniformly invertible local models and singular or poorly bounded selections.

assumptions_latex: Let \(e_k=x_k-\bar x\). The Newton-type model \(V_k\) is invertible, with \(\kappa_k=\|V_k^{-1}\|\).
The aggregate local modeling and solve defect is \(r_k\), with \(\|r_k\|\le\rho_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimate certifies a negligible defect contribution when \(\kappa_k\rho_k=o(\|e_k\|)\); loss of this scaling marks the boundary at which the estimate no longer certifies Q-superlinear convergence.

notation.meaning: upper bound on the aggregate local defect

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate-certification boundary expressed through inverse amplification times an aggregate local-defect bound.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.4 Nonsingularity of Newton approximation p. 822
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The defect contribution to a perturbed Newton correction satisfies \[\|V_k^{-1}r_k\|\le\kappa_k\rho_k.\] Therefore, \(\kappa_k\rho_k=o(\|e_k\|)\) is sufficient for this contribution to be negligible at the Q-superlinear scale. If the available bound is only \(\kappa_k\rho_k=O(\|e_k\|)\), the estimate generally certifies at most a linear-scale contribution. If \(\kappa_k\rho_k\not\to0\), the estimate alone does not certify convergence to the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near singularity, inverse amplification multiplies the defect bound; superlinear behavior remains certified when the amplified defect is negligible relative to the current error, while weaker scaling loses that rate guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Singularity Transition Regimes

children.title: Failure of Semismooth Approximation
children.top_down_role: Directional irregularity or insufficient model accuracy for fast local behavior.

assumptions_latex: Use classical derivatives at differentiability points as Bouligand model selections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at zero but fails the semismooth approximation condition there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete scalar failure of semismooth approximation despite local Lipschitz continuity and directional differentiability.

source_refs.locator: 7.4 Nonsmooth Analysis II: Semismooth Functions p. 674
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping is locally Lipschitz at \(0\) and has directional derivative \(F'(0;d)=d\). For \(x\ne0\), \[F'(x)=1+2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x).\] Along \(x_j=(2\pi j)^{-1}\), one has \(F'(x_j)=0\) and \(F(x_j)=x_j\). Consequently, \[\frac{|F(x_j)-F(0)-F'(x_j)x_j|}{|x_j|}=1,\] so the generalized-derivative remainder is not \(o(|x_j|)\). The semismooth approximation needed for fast local Newton convergence therefore fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz, directionally differentiable scalar equation can have derivative selections whose normalized linearization error stays equal to one, violating semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Semismooth Approximation

children.title: Degenerate Active-Set Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local regimes where active pieces are not stably distinguished near a solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Active-Set Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes failure of locally stable active-set identification at a piecewise-smooth root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuous and admit finitely many local \(C^1\) selection functions \(F_i\), and define \(I(x)=\{i:F(x)=F_i(x)\}\). A root \(\bar x\) is in a degenerate active-set regime when \(|I(\bar x)|>1\) and, for every neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), there exist \(x,y\in U\) such that \(I(x)\ne I(y)\). Thus the active index set is not constant on any neighborhood of \(\bar x\), and local models chosen from active selections may switch among distinct active Jacobians.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root is in a degenerate active-set regime when several selections are active there and the active index set changes arbitrarily close to the root, preventing stable local active-set identification.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuous and admits finitely many local \(C^1\) selections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) on which \(I(x)\) is constant.

notation.meaning: indices of selection functions active at x

children.title: Active-Set Chattering
children.top_down_role: Repeated switching among active pieces during local iteration.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Chattering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines failure of finite active-piece identification along an iterative sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For iterates \(x_k\to\bar x\) of a method applied to a piecewise-smooth equation, let \(I_k=I(x_k)\). Active-set chattering occurs when \((I_k)\) is not eventually constant: for every \(K\), there exist \(k,\ell\ge K\) such that \(I_k\ne I_\ell\). If only finitely many active sets are possible, at least two distinct active sets then occur infinitely often, so the iteration does not finitely identify one local smooth piece.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chattering means that convergent iterates keep switching active sets indefinitely, so no single smooth piece is identified after finitely many iterations.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many local active sets occur.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I_k)\) is not eventually constant, and at least two active sets recur infinitely often.

notation.meaning: active index set at iterate k

children.title: Active-Piece Identification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Local boundaries separating stable identification from persistent switching.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Piece Identification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the geometric boundary condition obstructing robust local piece identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For selection regions \(R_i=\{x:F(x)=F_i(x)\}\), a root \(\bar x\) lies on an active-piece identification boundary when there exist distinct indices \(i\) and \(j\) such that \(\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}R_i\cap\operatorname{cl}R_j\), while neither \(R_i\) nor \(R_j\) contains a neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Equivalently, arbitrarily small perturbations of \(\bar x\) can enter different selection regions, so identification cannot be robust to unrestricted local perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An identification boundary is a root approached by at least two distinct selection regions, with neither region occupying an entire neighborhood of the root.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has finitely many local selection regions \(R_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}R_i\cap\operatorname{cl}R_j\) for some \(i\ne j\), with no locally dominant region.

notation.meaning: region on which selection i represents the mapping

children.title: Nonisolated-Root Drift
children.top_down_role: Loss of pointwise convergence or unstable branch selection near nonisolated solution sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated-Root Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A linear example showing why residual convergence need not imply convergence to one root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\) by \(F(x,y)=(x,0)\). Its root set is \(S=\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb{R}\}\). The Newton equation \(F'(x_k,y_k)d_k=-F(x_k,y_k)\) imposes only \((d_k)_1=-x_k\), leaving \((d_k)_2\) arbitrary. Hence updates \((x_{k+1},y_{k+1})=(0,y_k+\eta_k)\) have zero residual after one step, but a nonconvergent choice of \((\eta_k)\) causes drift along \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonisolated line of roots, Newton equations leave a tangential step free; residuals can vanish while iterates drift and fail to converge pointwise.
assumptions_latex: The Newton system is solved without a rule fixing its null-space component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|F(x_k,y_k)\|=0\) may hold eventually while \((x_k,y_k)\) fails to converge.

children.title: Representation-Induced Ill-Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Numerical instability caused by a poorly scaled or intrinsically ill-conditioned residual representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Induced Ill-Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that equivalent residual equations can have arbitrarily different numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=x\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and for \(0<\varepsilon\le1\) set \(A_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon,1,\ldots,1)\) and \(R_\varepsilon(x)=A_\varepsilon F(x)\). Because \(A_\varepsilon\) is nonsingular, \(R_\varepsilon(x)=0\) and \(F(x)=0\) have the same unique root. Nevertheless, \(\kappa_2(R_\varepsilon')=\kappa_2(A_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon^{-1}\), and \(\|R_\varepsilon(x)\|_2\) suppresses error in the first coordinate by the factor \(\varepsilon\). Thus residual representation alone can create arbitrary ill-conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsingular scaling preserves the root but can make the residual Jacobian arbitrarily ill-conditioned and hide error in selected coordinates.
assumptions_latex: Conditioning is measured in the Euclidean operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-1}(0)=R_\varepsilon^{-1}(0)\) while \(\kappa_2(R_\varepsilon')=\varepsilon^{-1}\to\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source reference or locator is supplied for this nontrivial conditioning claim.

children.title: Residual-Norm Merits
children.top_down_role: Scalar merits constructed directly from equation residuals.

children.title: Norm Residual Merits
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth scalar residual measures based on general norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm Residual Merits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines scalar equation merits induced by arbitrary norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb{R}^m\). The norm residual merit is \(\phi(x)=\|F(x)\|\). It satisfies \(\phi(x)\ge0\) and \(\phi(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\). Consequently, every global minimizer attaining value zero is a root, and every root is a global minimizer of \(\phi\). If \(F\) is locally Lipschitz, then \(\phi\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The norm of the equation residual is a nonnegative merit function whose zero-valued points are exactly the roots.

children.title: Squared-Residual Merits
children.top_down_role: Least-squares residual merits and their local differentiability structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Squared-Residual Merits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the basic certificate and Clarke differential structure of least-squares residual merit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For locally Lipschitz \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), define \(\psi(x)=\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\). Then \(\psi\) is locally Lipschitz, nonnegative, and \(\psi(x)=0\) exactly when \(F(x)=0\). Clarke's chain rule gives \(\partial_C\psi(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{V^{\mathsf T}F(x):V\in\partial_C F(x)\}\). If \(F\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(\psi\) is differentiable there and \(\nabla\psi(x)=F'(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared Euclidean residual has the same zeros as the equation and admits a generalized-gradient formula, reducing to the usual least-squares gradient at differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\psi^{-1}(0)=F^{-1}(0)\) and \(\partial_C\psi(x)\subseteq\operatorname{co}\{V^{\mathsf T}F(x):V\in\partial_C F(x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Residual Merits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines quadratic residual merits using a positive-definite output-space metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be symmetric positive definite. The weighted residual merit is \(\phi_W(x)=\tfrac12F(x)^{\mathsf T}WF(x)=\tfrac12\|W^{1/2}F(x)\|_2^2\). Positive definiteness implies \(\phi_W(x)\ge0\) and \(\phi_W(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\). Moreover, \(\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(W)\|F(x)\|_2^2\le\phi_W(x)\le\tfrac12\lambda_{\max}(W)\|F(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite weight defines an equivalent squared residual merit while emphasizing different residual components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_W^{-1}(0)=F^{-1}(0)\), with spectral bounds determined by \(W\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Residual Merits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes weighted merits to componentwise positive residual scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=(F_1,\ldots,F_m):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and choose scales \(s_i>0\). With \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\), the scaled residual merit is \(\phi_S(x)=\tfrac12\|S^{-1}F(x)\|_2^2=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m(F_i(x)/s_i)^2\). Since every scale is finite and positive, \(\phi_S(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\). The scales alter component balance but not the certified solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive component scales normalize residual coordinates and preserve exactly the equation's zero set.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning-Sensitive Residual Merits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures residual through the inverse of a nonsingular local equation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(V(x)\) be a selected nonsingular local derivative model. The conditioning-sensitive residual merit is \(\phi_V(x)=\tfrac12\|V(x)^{-1}F(x)\|_2^2\). It measures the norm of the model Newton correction rather than the unscaled residual. For fixed nonsingular \(V(x)\), \(\phi_V(x)=0\) if and only if \(F(x)=0\); however, small singular values of \(V(x)\) strongly amplify associated residual components, exposing local model ill-conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This merit measures the predicted Newton correction, amplifying residual components associated with poorly conditioned model directions while preserving the root certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(V(x)\) is nonsingular wherever the merit is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi_V(x)=0\iff F(x)=0\), and \(\phi_V\) increases along residual directions amplified by \(V(x)^{-1}\).

children.title: Fischer–Burmeister Merits
children.top_down_role: Merit constructions associated with Fischer–Burmeister residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Fischer–Burmeister Merits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents componentwise complementarity by a squared Fischer–Burmeister residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\varphi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}-a-b\). Then \(\varphi_{\mathrm{FB}}(a,b)=0\) if and only if \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(ab=0\). For mappings \(G,H:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), set \(\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)_i=\varphi_{\mathrm{FB}}(G_i(x),H_i(x))\) and \(\Psi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=\tfrac12\|\Phi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)\|_2^2\). Hence \(\Psi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\) exactly when every pair \((G_i(x),H_i(x))\) satisfies complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared Fischer–Burmeister residual is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at componentwise complementary pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Psi_{\mathrm{FB}}(x)=0\iff 0\le G(x)\perp H(x)\ge0\).

children.title: Implicit-Lagrangian Merits
children.top_down_role: Implicit-Lagrangian merit families for nonlinear complementarity systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit-Lagrangian Merits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal value-function interpretation for finite-dimensional nonlinear complementarity problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) and \(c>0\). For \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\), define the implicit value merit
\[\Psi_c(x):=\max_{y\in\mathbb R_+^n}\left\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac c2\lVert x-y\rVert^2\right\}.\]
Its unique auxiliary maximizer is \(y_c(x)=P_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x-F(x)/c)\). Hence \(\Psi_c(x)\geq0\), and \(\Psi_c(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\geq0\), \(F(x)\geq0\), and \(\langle x,F(x)\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal auxiliary value is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at complementary feasible pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Psi_c(x)=0\iff 0\leq x\perp F(x)\geq0\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the nonnegative orthant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas are mathematically consistent with the regularized gap specialized to the nonnegative orthant, but no source supports identifying this construction as an implicit-Lagrangian merit under the target terminology.

children.title: Complementarity-Merit Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Relationships between merit stationarity, complementarity solutions, and nonroot stationary points.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity-Merit Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution stationarity and failure of its converse for the proximal complementarity merit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F\) is continuously differentiable, the merit \(\Psi_c\) is continuously differentiable and
\[\nabla\Psi_c(x)=F(x)+\bigl(DF(x)^{\mathsf T}-cI\bigr)\bigl(x-y_c(x)\bigr).\]
Every complementarity solution satisfies \(\nabla\Psi_c(x)=0\). The converse can fail: for \(n=1\), \(F(x)=(x-1)^2+1\), and \(c>1\), the interior point \(x=1\) has \(y_c(1)=1-1/c\), \(\Psi_c'(1)=0\), and \(\Psi_c(1)=1/(2c)>0\), so it is not complementary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every complementarity solution is merit-stationary, but merit stationarity can occur at a positive, nonzero merit value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq x\perp F(x)\geq0\Rightarrow\nabla\Psi_c(x)=0\), while the converse is false in general.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gradient calculation and scalar nonroot-stationarity example are correct for the preceding proximal merit, but the record lacks evidence for the merit convention and associated stationarity claim.

children.title: Projection-Based Regularized Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regularized gaps represented through projection-type auxiliary problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Regularized Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean regularization for a variational inequality on a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\). For \(c>0\), the regularized gap is
\[g_c(x):=\max_{y\in K}\left\{\langle F(x),x-y\rangle-\frac c2\lVert x-y\rVert^2\right\},\qquad x\in K.\]
The maximizer is unique and equals \(y_c(x)=P_K(x-F(x)/c)\). Consequently,
\[g_c(x)=\langle F(x),x-y_c(x)\rangle-\frac c2\lVert x-y_c(x)\rVert^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly concave auxiliary problem represents the regularized gap through one Euclidean projection.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_c(x)=P_K(x-F(x)/c)\) and the displayed projection formula holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized-Gap Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Envelope smoothness despite possible nondifferentiability of the projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the projection-based definition of \(g_c\), continuity of \(F\) implies continuity of \(g_c\). If \(F\) is locally Lipschitz, then \(g_c\) is locally Lipschitz. If \(F\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(K\), uniqueness of \(y_c(x)\) yields
\[\nabla g_c(x)=F(x)+\bigl(DF(x)^{\mathsf T}-cI\bigr)\bigl(x-y_c(x)\bigr)\]
at every interior point \(x\) of \(K\), even where the projection mapping is not differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized gap inherits continuity or local Lipschitzness from the mapping and becomes smooth when the mapping is smooth.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has the regularity specified in each conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in C^1\Rightarrow g_c\in C^1\) on \(\operatorname{int}K\), with the displayed gradient.

children.title: Regularized-Gap Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Relationships between stationary points, variational-inequality solutions, and spurious stationary points.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized-Gap Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained stationarity is necessary at VI solutions but insufficient for solutionhood without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(U\supseteq K\) be open, and let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable. Using the same maximization formula to extend \(g_c\) to \(U\), every solution \(x^*\) of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\) satisfies \(y_c(x^*)=x^*\), \(g_c(x^*)=0\), and
\[0\in\nabla g_c(x^*)+N_K(x^*).\]
If \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}K\), then \(F(x^*)=0\) and hence \(\nabla g_c(x^*)=0\). The converse fails even without a boundary: for \(K=\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=x^2+1\), and \(c>0\),
\[g_c(x)=\frac{(x^2+1)^2}{2c}.\]
Thus \(g_c'(0)=0\) and \(g_c(0)>0\), while \(\operatorname{VI}(\mathbb R,F)\), equivalently \(F(x)=0\), has no solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every VI solution is a constrained stationary zero of the regularized gap, and an interior solution has zero gradient; nevertheless, a zero-gradient point can have positive gap value and fail to solve the VI.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(U\supseteq K\) is open and \(F:U\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\Rightarrow 0\in\nabla g_c(x^*)+N_K(x^*)\); for \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}K\), \(\nabla g_c(x^*)=0\), but zero-gradient stationarity does not imply solutionhood.

children.title: Linearized Gap Functions

knowledge_statements.title: Linearized Gap Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unregularized gap generated by the affine variational model at the current point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\). The linearized gap function is
\[g_0(x):=\max_{y\in K}\langle F(x),x-y\rangle=\langle F(x),x\rangle-\min_{y\in K}\langle F(x),y\rangle.\]
It satisfies \(g_0(x)\geq0\). Moreover, \(g_0(x)=0\) if and only if \(\langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(y\in K\), so its zeros are precisely the solutions of \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing the current affine VI residual over a compact feasible set gives an exact nonnegative gap.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_0(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\).

notation.meaning: variational inequality on K with mapping F

children.title: D-Gap Parameter Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: D-Gap Parameter Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering, residual bounds, and coalescing-parameter limit for Euclidean D-gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0<a<b\), define \(G_{a,b}(x):=g_a(x)-g_b(x)\). Then
\[0\leq\frac{b-a}{2}\lVert x-y_b(x)\rVert^2\leq G_{a,b}(x)\leq\frac{b-a}{2}\lVert x-y_a(x)\rVert^2.\]
Thus the order \(a<b\) makes the D-gap nonnegative. For fixed \(a>0\), continuity of the projection path and the envelope derivative with respect to the regularization parameter give
\[\lim_{b\downarrow a}\frac{G_{a,b}(x)}{b-a}=\frac12\lVert x-y_a(x)\rVert^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordered parameters produce a nonnegative D-gap bounded by projected residuals, with a residual-squared limit as the parameters merge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_{a,b}\geq0\) with the displayed bounds and coalescing-parameter limit.

knowledge_statements.title: D-Gap Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smoothness obtained by subtracting two regularized-gap envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0<a<b\). If \(F\) is locally Lipschitz, then \(G_{a,b}=g_a-g_b\) is locally Lipschitz. If \(F\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(K\), then \(G_{a,b}\) is continuously differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}K\), with
\[\nabla G_{a,b}(x)=\bigl(DF(x)^{\mathsf T}-aI\bigr)(x-y_a(x))-\bigl(DF(x)^{\mathsf T}-bI\bigr)(x-y_b(x)).\]
The two explicit \(F(x)\) terms in the regularized-gap gradients cancel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The D-gap is locally Lipschitz for locally Lipschitz mappings and continuously differentiable for continuously differentiable mappings.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has the regularity specified in each conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in C^1\Rightarrow G_{a,b}\in C^1\) on \(\operatorname{int}K\), with the displayed gradient.

children.title: D-Gap Stationary Points

knowledge_statements.title: D-Gap Stationary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity conditions for a smooth D-gap on a closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(U\supseteq K\) be open, let \(F:U\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(0<a<b\). Define the natural extension of each regularized gap to \(U\) by the same maximization over \(K\). An interior point \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) is stationary for \(G_{a,b}\) precisely when
\[\bigl(DF(x)^{\mathsf T}-aI\bigr)(x-y_a(x))=\bigl(DF(x)^{\mathsf T}-bI\bigr)(x-y_b(x)).\]
A point \(x\in K\), including a boundary point, is constrained stationary precisely when
\[0\in\nabla G_{a,b}(x)+N_K(x),\]
where \(N_K(x)\) is the convex normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior D-gap stationarity balances the two projected residual models; constrained stationarity adds the feasible-set normal cone, using the gap's ambient smooth extension.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(U\supseteq K\) is open and \(F:U\to\mathbb R^n\) is continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed equality characterizes interior stationarity, while \(0\in\nabla G_{a,b}(x)+N_K(x)\) characterizes constrained stationarity on \(K\).

knowledge_statements.title: D-Gap Solution Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact zero-value characterization of variational-inequality solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(F:K\to\mathbb R^n\), and choose \(0<a<b\). For every \(x\in K\),
\[G_{a,b}(x)=0\iff x=y_a(x)\iff x=y_b(x)\iff \langle F(x),y-x\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for all }y\in K.\]
Therefore the verifiable scalar equality \(G_{a,b}(x)=0\) certifies that \(x\) solves \(\operatorname{VI}(K,F)\); equivalently, either projected residual vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A D-gap value is zero exactly at VI solutions, equivalently when either associated projected residual vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_{a,b}(x)=0\iff x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonroot D-Gap Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth one-dimensional D-gap can have a positive stationary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take \(K=\mathbb R\), \(F(x)=x^2+1\), and \(0<a<b\). Then \(y_c(x)=x-F(x)/c\), and
\[G_{a,b}(x)=\frac12\left(\frac1a-\frac1b\right)(x^2+1)^2.\]
Consequently, \(G_{a,b}'(0)=0\) while
\[G_{a,b}(0)=\frac12\left(\frac1a-\frac1b\right)>0.\]
Because \(\operatorname{VI}(\mathbb R,F)\) is equivalent to \(F(x)=0\), it has no solution. Thus \(x=0\) is a nonroot stationary point of the D-gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive stationary D-gap occurs for the scalar mapping x squared plus one, although its VI has no solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_{a,b}'(0)=0\) and \(G_{a,b}(0)>0\), so stationarity does not imply a VI solution.

children.title: Zero-Value Solution Certificates
children.top_down_role: Exact correspondence between vanishing merit values and target solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Value Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract exactness criterion shared by equation, complementarity, and variational-inequality merits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a set, let \(S\subseteq X\) be the target solution set, and let \(m:X\to[0,+\infty]\). If
\[m(x)=0\iff x\in S,\]
then the equality \(m(x)=0\) is an exact zero-value solution certificate. For a computable residual map \(R:X\to\mathbb R^q\), the stronger representation
\[\alpha\lVert R(x)\rVert^p\leq m(x)\leq\beta\lVert R(x)\rVert^p\]
with \(p>0\) and \(0<\alpha\leq\beta\) verifies exactness whenever \(S=R^{-1}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative merit is an exact certificate when its zero set equals the target solution set; residual bounds verify this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m^{-1}(0)=S\); two-sided positive residual bounds imply this equality when \(S=R^{-1}(0)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuous, let \(S:=F^{-1}(0)\neq\varnothing\), and define \(\phi(x):=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert^2\). Given \(\bar x\in S\) and a neighborhood \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) of \(\bar x\), suppose there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq \kappa\lVert F(x)\rVert=\kappa\sqrt{2\phi(x)}\qquad(x\in U).\]
Then the merit value certifies that every \(x\in U\) lies within distance \(\kappa\sqrt{2\phi(x)}\) of \(S\). In particular, for every \(\varepsilon\geq0\),
\[\phi(x)\leq\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2\kappa^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local residual error bound converts the square root of the equation merit into a certified upper bound on distance to the solution set; a sufficiently small merit value therefore certifies any prescribed nonnegative distance tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Merit Error Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous and bounded below, and, for each \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), define
\[L_\alpha:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\phi(x)\leq\alpha\}.\]
The function \(\phi\) is coercive, meaning that \(\phi(x_j)\to+\infty\) for every sequence \((x_j)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\lVert x_j\rVert\to\infty\), if and only if \(L_\alpha\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). If a sequence \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(\phi(x_{k+1})\leq\phi(x_k)\) for every \(k\geq0\), then \(x_k\in L_{\phi(x_0)}\) for every \(k\geq0\). Hence the sequence is bounded whenever its initial sublevel set is bounded, even when \(\phi\) is noncoercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, coercivity is equivalent to boundedness of every merit sublevel set, while a merit-nonincreasing sequence is bounded as soon as its initial sublevel set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Level-Set Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and define \(\phi(y):=\tfrac12\lVert F(y)\rVert^2\) for \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Suppose a local Newton model selects \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(Vd=-F(x)\), and suppose the compatibility condition \(F'(x;d)=Vd\) holds. Then
\[\phi'(x;d)=\langle F(x),F'(x;d)\rangle=-\lVert F(x)\rVert^2=-2\phi(x).\]
Consequently, if \(F(x)\neq0\), then \(d\) is a strict descent direction for \(\phi\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the selected Newton matrix and direction reproduce the directional derivative and solve the exact local Newton equation, then the squared-residual merit has directional derivative equal to minus the squared residual and therefore strictly decreases at every nonroot.
knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Direction Descent Compatibility

children.title: Nonroot Stationary Points
children.top_down_role: Stationary points of equation merits that do not certify roots of the underlying system.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonroot Stationary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth one-dimensional counterexample showing that merit stationarity need not certify an equation root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(F(x):=x^2-1\) and its equation merit \(\phi(x):=\tfrac12(F(x))^2=\tfrac12(x^2-1)^2\). Direct differentiation yields \(\phi'(x)=2x(x^2-1)\). Hence \(\phi'(0)=0\), equivalently \(0\in\partial_C\phi(0)\), although \(F(0)=-1\neq0\). Thus \(x=0\) is a stationary point of the smooth, nonnegative merit but is not a root of the underlying equation. The failure occurs because stationarity only imposes \(F'(x)^{\mathsf T}F(x)=0\), which need not force \(F(x)=0\) when the Jacobian is rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared merit of the equation x²−1=0 is stationary at zero, although zero is not a root, because the Jacobian vanishes there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial_C\phi(0)\) while \(F(0)\neq0\).
